title: The Clock of the Palatinate
premise: In 1918, Tamsin Amberdale drives for a suffragist organizer in the Rhineland town of Alsenborn, quietly reading every letter that passes through their hands. When the occupying army requisitions the town, it also seizes the ledger holding every name the movement ever recorded — names now marked as collaborators by the victors' historians. Tamsin must steal the ledger back and get its truth notarized before the official record hardens into history. They succeed at terrible cost: the ledger survives, but Tamsin's mentor is arrested in their place, and Tamsin learns that belonging to a cause means carrying what cannot be carried alone.
about_author: Astrid Zhou is a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing occupation-era correspondence in European municipal collections. She writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. We meet them reading letters in the motorcar while their employer, Frau Voss, organizes women across the Palatinate — and keeping a private mental ledger of every secret entrusted to paper. The army arrives to requisition Alsenborn, including the movement's records. Beat: quiet competence curdling into dread as Tamsin realizes the names are evidence now.

chapters.title: The Requisitioned House
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The army billets officers in the movement's headquarters; the ledger is crated for transport to the victors' archives. Tamsin charms a young clerk into revealing the shipping schedule while wrestling with guilt over using someone again. Beat: rising tension — the plan forms, but betrayal feels like survival's price.

chapters.title: Notarized by Candlelight
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, climax. On the night before shipment, Tamsin steals the ledger with Frau Voss's help, but the diversion goes wrong and soldiers catch Voss covering Tamsin's escape. At a notary's back room, Tamsin swears the record true page by page until dawn. Beat: triumph braided with grief — the truth is on the record, bought with a person.

chapters.title: The Victor's Historians
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, months later. The official histories appear and contradict the ledger; Tamsin distributes certified copies to families across the Palatinate, watching names reclaim themselves. Voss remains imprisoned, her sentence commuted but unresolved. Tamsin takes up her route, reading letters still. Beat: bittersweet resolution — belonging means continuing the work.
